candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — monitoring equipment, alarm safety and error prevention
candidate.educational_objective: Apply individualized, policy-consistent physiologic alarm settings to reduce nonactionable alarms without compromising patient safety.

options.A: Leave every default limit unchanged even when it produces repeated nonactionable alarms.
options.B: Silence the alarm permanently so it cannot recur.
options.C: Tailor alarm limits to the individual client's clinical condition within approved policy while preserving clinically meaningful alerts.
options.D: Disable all physiologic alarms whenever the client has a chronic abnormal baseline.

candidate.rationale: AHRQ patient-safety guidance identifies alarm settings that are not tailored to individual patients as a contributor to alarm fatigue and recommends tailoring alarm thresholds when default settings do not fit the patient's clinical baseline. Alarms should remain clinically meaningful rather than being permanently silenced. Therefore C is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Default alarm settings may not fit an individual patient; clinicians can tailor alarm thresholds to the individual clinical baseline to reduce excessive nonactionable alarms, while alarms should not simply be silenced.
candidate.source_locator: What can be done to combat alarm fatigue?; Take-Home Points — tailor alarm thresholds to the individual patient
candidate.source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) PSNet
candidate.stem: A nurse is caring for a monitored client whose usual heart rate is above the unit's default high-alarm threshold. Which approach best supports alarm safety?
